Martin Luther King Jr. On April 4, 1968, Dr. Martin Luther King Jr., the preeminent leader of the American Civil Rights Movement, was shot and killed on the balcony of the Lorraine Motel in Memphis, Tennessee.

King was shot by James Earl Ray, a career criminal and low-level racist with a grudge. Ray fired from a rooming house across the street using a .30-06 rifle. King was pronounced dead at St. Joseph's Hospital. He was thirty-nine years old.

King was in Memphis to support a sanitation workers' strike and to plan the Poor People's Campaign. Ray's motive remained unclear—whether he was motivated purely by racism, by payment from unidentified parties, or by Cold War paranoia about King's radicalism. Ray was apprehended in London weeks later and extradited to the United States. He spent decades in prison and died in 1998. The true extent of any conspiracy, if one existed, remains debated.

King's death triggered weeks of rioting in more than one hundred American cities. The country grieved and raged simultaneously. Congress passed the Civil Rights Act of 1968, also known as the Fair Housing Act, just days after his death, a legislative legacy. The assassination accelerated a shift in the civil rights movement toward more militant Black nationalist movements and away from nonviolent integration.

King's assassination stands as the definitive moment when the Civil Rights Movement, at the height of its moral authority under his leadership, was fractured by a single violent act. Unlike Lincoln's or Kennedy's deaths, King was killed for explicitly challenging American racism—shot for preaching nonviolence and demanding justice. The event exposed the vulnerability of moral suasion to violence and deepened a national wound. It marked a symbolic end to the optimistic, legislative phase of civil rights from 1954 to 1968 and inaugurated the era of Black Power, institutional racism studies, and more fragmented, community-based activism. The year 1968 saw not only King's death but also the assassination of Robert Kennedy just two months later, an eruption of violence that shook the nation and defined a generation.
